subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Non Examination Assessment Spoken Language Endorsement
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the assessment objectives.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which is the best example of 'colloquial' language?
options: The committee will reconvene at noon.
I am writing to inform you of the situation.
I should be most grateful for your assistance.
questions.explain: Colloquial language is informal, everyday speech, often using slang like 'mate' and 'well good'.

questions.q: Which sentence uses 'non-standard' rather than Standard English?
options: We had not been there yesterday.
questions.explain: 'We wasn't' is non-standard; Standard English requires 'we weren't'.

options: Only the language used in poems
The variety of English widely accepted as correct in formal contexts
questions.explain: Standard English is the form recognised as correct for formal and official communication.

questions.q: Which feature is typical of spontaneous spoken language but not planned writing?
options: Fillers and false starts like 'um, I mean, the thing is...'
questions.explain: Spontaneous speech often contains fillers, false starts and self-correction.

questions.q: Which statement about regional dialect words is true?
options: They reflect local variation and identity, like 'bairn' for child in the North East
They are the same as RP
They can only be written, never spoken
questions.explain: Dialect words show regional variation and identity and are a legitimate part of language.

questions.q: What does it mean to say language 'changes over time'?
options: Words, meanings and usage shift across generations, with new words added and others fading
questions.explain: Language evolves as new words appear, meanings shift and some terms become archaic.

options: A prestige accent traditionally associated with Standard English and the BBC
questions.explain: RP is a prestige, non-regional accent historically linked to Standard English and broadcasting.

questions.q: Why might a speaker change their language depending on their audience?
options: To make speech harder to follow
To suit the level of formality and ensure they are understood
questions.explain: Speakers adapt register and vocabulary to match context and audience for clarity and appropriateness.

questions.q: Which is a feature of an effective spoken presentation?
options: Clear pacing, eye contact and varied tone to engage the audience
Reading every word in a flat monotone
questions.explain: Good presentations use pacing, eye contact and vocal variety to hold attention.

questions.q: In a job interview, which language choice is most appropriate?
options: Specialist jargon the interviewer won't know
Standard English with a polite, formal register
questions.explain: Formal contexts like interviews call for Standard English and a polite register.

options: Informal words and phrases often used by particular groups, e.g. 'lit', 'peng'
questions.explain: Slang is very informal language, often group-specific and changing quickly.

options: A variety of language used by a particular social group
A language used only in writing
A formal speech given to a council
questions.explain: A sociolect is the distinctive language of a social group, shaped by factors like age or class.
